Artifact 1

Small Business Dashboard Assistant

An AI assistant that turns a small business’s sales data into a working dashboard

Summary

Small business owners usually have sales data sitting in Square, Shopify, or a spreadsheet, but no analyst to turn it into something useful. I built an AI assistant in ChatGPT that fills that gap.

The owner uploads a sales file, and the assistant asks a few simple questions about what they want to see, confirms the plan, and then builds a working dashboard. Every number is calculated directly from the owner’s data, and it never makes numbers up.

Objective

Help non-technical business owners see how their business is doing, using data they already have, without learning BI tools or hiring an analyst.

Tools and technologies used

  • ChatGPT Plugin Creator
  • Python
  • HTML and CSS
  • Chart.js
  • Microsoft Excel
  • Kaggle Superstore data

Process

  1. Understand the user. I focused on small business owners who have sales data but no time or tools to analyze it.
  2. Plan the assistant. I defined what it should do, what it should never do, like invent numbers, and the steps it follows.
  3. Build it. I created the assistant as a ChatGPT plugin with clear instructions and a sample data file.
  4. Test and improve. I tested every rule and improved the assistant across three versions.
  5. Verify the numbers. I checked the dashboard totals against the original data in Excel, and every number matched.

How it improved

Version 1

The workflow worked, but it described the data in technical terms a shop owner would not understand.

Version 2

Plain language fixed the conversation, but the charts failed to load on first delivery.

Version 3

Charts work offline, the layout stays simple, and every number matches the source data.

Challenges and solutions

Technical language

Challenge: The first version described the data in analyst terms like “product-line records” that a shop owner would not understand.

Solution: I rewrote its instructions in plain language and listed the exact technical words to avoid.

Blank charts

Challenge: The second version’s charts did not load because my instructions told it to use an outside link for the chart library.

Solution: I changed the instructions to build the chart library into the dashboard file so it works offline.

Platform change

Challenge: OpenAI retired custom GPTs while I was building the assistant.

Solution: I moved the design to ChatGPT’s new plugin format without changing how the assistant works.

Dashboard output

Value proposition

This project shows I can take a real business need from idea to a working AI tool: understand the user, design the conversation, test every rule, and verify the results against the source data.

See the assistant in action

Artifact 2

Machine Learning vs. Deep Learning

Choosing the right approach, explained through two projects from my own work

Summary

Machine learning and deep learning are both part of artificial intelligence, but they learn from data in different ways. In traditional machine learning, people decide which features matter and feed them into a model. In deep learning, multi-layered neural networks find those features on their own from raw data.

To compare the two, I used two projects from my work in telecommunications: a model that predicts customer trouble calls, built with traditional machine learning, and a voice-enabled chatbot that answers data questions in plain English, powered by deep learning.

Objective

Show when each approach is the right choice, and why, using real business problems instead of textbook definitions.

Side-by-side comparison

Trouble call prediction (machine learning)Data chatbot (deep learning)
Lesson exampleCustomer churn predictionNatural language processing with transformer models
The problemRank customer accounts by how likely they are to call with a service problem, so field teams can act firstLet business users ask data questions out loud, in plain English, without knowing SQL
The dataStructured rows and columns: signal levels, network structure, outage history, past call reasonsUnstructured speech and text, asked in many different ways
FeaturesChosen by people with domain expertiseLearned automatically by neural networks
OutputAn explainable risk score for each accountA generated SQL query and an answer
Why the other approach would not fitDeep learning would add cost and complexity with no real accuracy gain, and its black-box scores would be harder for operations teams to trustNo one can hand-build features for every way a question can be phrased, and traditional models predict labels or numbers rather than generating language

Example 1: Trouble call prediction

A trouble call happens when a customer contacts the company because something is wrong with their service. The goal was to predict which accounts were likely to call, so field operations could fix problems before customers noticed. I supported the project by preparing the data, while the machine learning team built the model.

The model was trained on two to three years of labeled history, comparing accounts that had trouble calls with those that did not. It used features that domain experts already knew mattered, such as signal levels, network structure, outages, and past call reasons. Because the data was structured and the scores needed to be explained to the teams acting on them, traditional machine learning was the right fit.

Example 2: Voice-enabled data chatbot

I built a chatbot that lets a business user ask a question out loud and get an answer from the data warehouse, without writing SQL or knowing which tables to use. Every stage relies on deep learning:

You ask a question out loud
“How many outages did my region have last week?”
↓
Speech to Text
Voice · Accents · Converted to text
↓
Orchestrator
LangGraph · Routes each step of the workflow
⇅
Vector Database (RAG)
Business docs · Rules · Table metadata
Large Language Model
AWS Bedrock · Writes SQL using that context
⇅
Data Warehouse
Runs the query · Returns results
↓
Plain-Language Answer
Sent back to the user · No SQL needed

Conceptual architecture, simplified. No proprietary details.

People speak with different accents and speeds and phrase the same question many ways. Speech recognition, embeddings, and language models are all deep neural networks trained on huge amounts of audio and text, which is why they can handle that variety.

Process

  1. Pick the lesson examples. I chose customer churn prediction for machine learning and transformer-based language models for deep learning.
  2. Match them to real work. I connected each one to a project I worked on.
  3. Analyze the fit. For each project, I explained why its approach worked and why the other would not.
  4. Draw the lesson. I summarized what the comparison taught me about choosing an approach.

Tools and technologies used

  • Classical ML models
  • Large language models
  • Speech-to-text
  • Vector database
  • RAG
  • AWS Bedrock
  • LangGraph

Challenges and solutions

Giving the chatbot business context

Challenge: A language model on its own has no idea what the company’s tables mean or how the business defines things, so it would guess.

Solution: We embedded business documentation, rules, and table descriptions in a vector database and retrieved the relevant pieces with each question (RAG), so the SQL matches the real data.

Trust in prediction scores

Challenge: Operations teams need to understand why an account is flagged before they act on it.

Solution: Using traditional machine learning on known features kept the risk scores explainable.

Value proposition

Many teams reach for the newest AI by default. This project shows that I can match the approach to the problem: traditional machine learning when the data is structured and the results must be explained, and deep learning when the input is messy language that no one can capture with hand-built rules. Neither approach is better in general. The right one depends on the data and the problem.

Artifact 3

Leading AI Change: My Leadership Self-Assessment

Where I stand as a leader of AI and data change, and where I am growing

Summary

Most professionals never stop to measure their own leadership skills. I completed two self-assessments, one on leading AI/ML integration and one on change management, and rated myself honestly against my real work experience building dashboards, AI chatbots, and automated workflows.

I then reflected on my strongest and weakest areas and proposed changes to the assessments themselves, based on what I have learned leading AI projects in practice.

Selected categories shown.

Strengths and growth areas

My strengths

  • Technical understanding of AI, from building chatbots and connecting AI to business systems
  • Stakeholder communication and gathering continuous feedback from users
  • Critical thinking and problem-solving

Where I am growing

  • Ethical and responsible AI governance
  • Formal change management knowledge
  • Leading people through larger organizational transitions

Challenges and solutions

Rating myself honestly

Challenge: My first ratings undersold the hands-on AI work I had already done, like building chatbots and AI workflows.

Solution: I re-rated each category against concrete examples from my work, so the scores reflect real experience rather than guesses.

Gaps in the assessment itself

Challenge: The AI/ML assessment did not ask about data quality, system integration, or educating users, which matter most in real AI projects.

Solution: I proposed new questions to cover those areas.

How I would improve the AI/ML assessment

From my own experience building AI tools, I would add questions on:

Data quality and governance

Enterprise data is huge, and without correct labeling and metadata, AI tools give unreliable or made-up answers.

Connecting systems

Real AI solutions depend on integrating different applications and services, not just on the model.

The business problem

A leader should first ask what the business is actually trying to solve before choosing AI.

Educating users

Helping people understand and adopt AI tools is a core part of leading AI change.

Objective and value

The objective was to measure my readiness to lead AI and change, and to create a growth plan from the results. For others, it shows that self-assessment is a practical first step in leadership, and the revisions offer ideas for evaluating AI leaders more realistically.
